summary: This is a humorous RFC. It notes that TLS 1.3 key derivation uses a string of zero bytes as input when no pre-shared key is in use, and it jokingly proposes replacing those zeros with a hash of the audio of 2 Live Crew's "Banned in the U.S.A.". It is Informational and not something to deploy.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9949 is an April 1st joke about changing one input in TLS 1.3 key derivation. It proposes using the hash of a specific song instead of zero bytes, while acknowledging that the song is not secret.

questions: why is tls zero bytes a problem
subtitle: An April 1st joke replaces TLS 1.3's zero-byte input with a song digest.

tldr.problem: This April 1st RFC calls the zero-byte input used at the start of TLS 1.3 key derivation an aesthetic problem, while noting that the operation is technically sound.
tldr.mechanism: It proposes replacing that input with the SHA-256 digest of raw PCM audio from 2 Live Crew's “Banned in the U.S.A.”.
tldr.outcome: Both peers would need the same recording to derive matching keys. The document is satire and says the audio is a non-secret constant.

today: RFC 9949 is an Informational document published on April 1, 2026. Its song-based key derivation proposal is humorous and is not a real TLS deployment specification.

sections.title: The “Zero-Byte Problem”
sections.content: In the PSK-free case described by TLS 1.3, the initial HKDF-Extract operation uses a string of zero bytes as input keying material. RFC 9949 calls this aesthetically troubling, while stating that the operation is technically fine. Its proposed replacement is the SHA-256 digest of raw PCM audio from “Banned in the U.S.A.” by 2 Live Crew.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS 1.3 can start this key derivation step with zero bytes. The joke proposes using a song's digest instead, not because the zero-byte method is technically broken.

sections.title: The Mandatory Audio Component
sections.content: The RFC defines the Mandatory Audio Component (MAC) as SHA-256 of the recording's raw PCM audio in a specified canonical form. It says both peers must use the same component or Finished-message verification fails. The document also says the MAC is a 32-byte value and is a constant, not secret key material.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides would need to derive the same digest from the specified recording. The RFC says the result is public and must not be treated as a secret.

sections.title: Security and the Satire
sections.content: The RFC states that the Mandatory Audio Component has zero entropy against an adversary who knows the recording and must not be treated as secret key material. It says BUSA-TLS is not intended for deployments that require confidentiality from a PSK component. The surrounding requirements and alerts are part of the document's April 1st humor.
sections.plainLanguage: The song digest is not secret, so it cannot provide secret key material. The RFC presents its proposal as a joke, not a replacement for TLS 1.3.
